analysis.one_liner: Bans lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers for harms caused when others criminally misuse their products.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have dismissed pending lawsuits against the gun industry, died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote, despite 62 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to sue firearm or ammunition makers, sellers, or their trade association in any federal or state court for damages caused when someone criminally misuses a gun. It would also have immediately thrown out every such lawsuit already in court on the day it was signed, including suits cities had filed against the industry. Only two narrow exceptions remained: suits against someone who knowingly handed a gun to a convicted violent or drug trafficker, and suits for negligent entrustment or negligence per se.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, distributors, importers, and their trade associations gain near-total protection from civil lawsuits arising from criminal misuse of their products, including the pending municipal suits seeking to recover the costs of gun violence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, dealers, and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any 'qualified civil liability action' against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, or trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of their products, in any federal or state court.
It requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit already pending on the date of enactment, wiping out existing claims against the industry.

It preserves two narrow exceptions: actions against someone convicted of knowingly transferring a firearm for a violent or drug trafficking crime, and actions against a seller for negligent entrustment or negligence per se.

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and their families, and cities and counties that had sued gun makers to recover the public costs of gun violence, would lose their access to the courts; the costs of gun violence would stay with victims, taxpayers, and health systems.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have closed the courthouse on plaintiffs whose cases were already pending, dismissing them immediately upon enactment — a retroactive loss of legal rights for victims and municipalities.

The exceptions are narrow: ordinary negligence claims and most theories used in municipal suits against the industry would be barred, leaving negligent distribution practices largely beyond judicial pressure and shifting gun-violence costs to victims and taxpayers.

Supporters' good-faith case was that the suits targeted lawful businesses for the acts of criminals, stretched liability beyond centuries of common law, and threatened a constitutionally protected right; an honest supporter would concede that the bill also preempted state tort law and eliminated a market pressure that might otherwise deter careless selling practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered the gun industry a litigation shield whose costs fell on shooting victims and on cities trying to recover public expenses — and it would have retroactively erased cases already in court. The narrow exceptions preserved little of the suits' deterrent value. On balance, its benefits went to a concentrated industry while its costs were spread across the public; its failure meant those costs were not imposed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on January 3, 2001, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Barr (R-GA) introduced the Firearms Heritage Protection Act of 2001 on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken.
It attracted 62 cosponsors: 50 House Republicans, 11 House Democrats, and the chamber's one Independent.

The bill would have barred civil suits against gun and ammunition makers and sellers for damages from criminal misuse of their products and required immediate dismissal of pending actions, with narrow exceptions for knowing transfers to criminals and negligent entrustment.
Because the bill never left committee, no lawsuit was dismissed and the pending municipal actions against the gun industry continued.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shooting victims, their families, and the municipalities pursuing lawsuits against gun makers kept their day in court, because the bill never got a vote. The gun industry, which sought immunity from those suits, did not get it in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-violence victims and the suing cities

for.name: Rep. Bob Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 107th Congress.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2001 and never reported the bill out — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; sponsorship leaned Republican (50 of 62 cosponsors) but included 11 House Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and importers
industries.note: The bill would have given the whole gun trade immunity from civil suits over criminal misuse of its products and wiped out the municipal lawsuits then pending against it. That shield would have removed both a financial cost of careless distribution practices and a legal pressure on them, with the remaining costs of gun violence left to victims, cities, and taxpayers.
Trade associations of gun sellers were named as protected defendants alongside manufacturers and sellers, exempting them from industry-wide liability suits.

industries.industry: State and local governments suing the gun industry
industries.note: Cities and municipalities had filed suits seeking to recover the public costs of gun violence; the bill would have dismissed those cases immediately, eliminating their main legal tool and leaving those costs on their budgets and their residents.

industries.industry: Trial lawyers and products-liability plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: A broad category of civil actions against gun sellers would have been barred in every court, removing a category of contingency-fee litigation and, with it, a private enforcement channel against negligent sales.
